procedural_history.impugned_order: Certificate granted under Article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution of India, allowing appeal to the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court granted a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) seemingly believing they had no option and misdirected themselves about the law, not exercising the discretion vested in them.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached because the appellants obtained a certificate from the High Court, and contended that the Supreme Court was bound to hear their case as an appellate court on both facts and law. The Supreme Court determined that the certificate was wrongly granted and treated the case as a petition for special leave under Article 136(1). The Supreme Court then dismissed the appeal, finding no reason to interfere with the High Court's findings and sentences.

decision.appeal_result: The appeal fails and is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the discretion of the High Court to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal under Article 134(1)(c) is a judicial discretion that must be exercised along well-established lines.

facts: The High Court granted a certificate for appeal under Article 134(1)(c) to two convicts.

The High Court did not believe their individual cases warranted a certificate but felt it was bound to grant one because it interpreted the word 'case' in the article to mean the appeal as a whole, which also included another person who was rightly granted a certificate.
This indicates the High Court believed it had no discretion in the matter regarding the two convicts, or that its discretion was fettered by its interpretation of the law.
law: The Supreme Court has general powers of judicial superintendence over all courts in India and is the ultimate interpreter and guardian of the Constitution.
The discretion granted to the High Court under Article 134(1)(c) is a judicial one.
This judicial discretion must be exercised along well-established lines that govern such matters.
The principles governing discretion under Article 134(1)(c) are the same as those under Article 133(1)(c), as they use the same language.
A certificate granted under this article must show on its face that the discretion was invoked and exercised.

The Supreme Court is not precluded from determining whether a certificate was rightly granted and whether the prerequisite conditions, including the proper exercise of judicial discretion, are satisfied.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had misdirected itself about the law by wrongly interpreting the word 'case' and believing it had no option but to grant the certificate to all convicts.
By considering its discretion to be fettered when it was not, the High Court failed to exercise the judicial discretion actually vested in it.
The Supreme Court asserted that when a lower court misdirects itself on a question of discretion, the superior court must interfere.

The Court established that if discretion is properly exercised, it will not interfere except on very strong grounds. However, in this instance, the discretion was not exercised at all due to a legal misdirection.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the issue, concluding that the High Court's power to grant a certificate of fitness for appeal under Article 134(1)(c) is not an absolute or unfettered power. Instead, it is a judicial discretion that must be exercised in accordance with well-established legal principles. When a High Court fails to exercise this discretion due to a misunderstanding of the law, the Supreme Court has a duty to intervene.

law.reasoning: However, this discretion is not absolute. It must be a "judicial one" and must be "judicially exercised along the well established lines which govern these matters."

law.reasoning: The Court's established practice of reviewing certificates under Article 133(1)(c) therefore applies equally to those under Article 134(1)(c).

application.fact: The mere grant of a certificate by the High Court does not prevent the Supreme Court from determining whether it was rightly granted and if the necessary conditions were met.
application.reasoning: Based on its supervisory role, the Court can review the High Court's exercise of discretion.

application.fact: The Supreme Court will not interfere with the High Court's decision if the discretion was properly exercised on well-established lines, except on very strong grounds.
application.reasoning: This shows deference to a proper exercise of judicial discretion.

application.fact: However, the Supreme Court must interfere if it is apparent that the High Court misdirected itself about the law or wrongly believed its discretion was fettered or non-existent.
application.reasoning: In such cases, the High Court has failed to properly exercise the judicial discretion vested in it, and the Supreme Court, as the superior court, must step in to correct the error.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that it has the authority to determine if a certificate of fitness for appeal granted by the High Court under Article 134(1)(c) was rightly granted. This authority stems from its role as the ultimate guardian of the Constitution and its power of judicial superintendence. It will review whether the High Court's judicial discretion was properly exercised and will interfere if the High Court misdirected itself on the law or failed to exercise its discretion.

issue.issue_text: Whether the grant of a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) automatically obligates the Supreme Court to hear the appeal on both facts and law, as an ordinary court of appeal.

facts: The appellants were granted a certificate by the High Court under Article 134(1)(c) to appeal to the Supreme Court.

The High Court granted the certificate under the mistaken belief that it was bound to do so for all convicts in the appeal, viewing the 'case' as the appeal as a whole, rather than the case of each individual.
The appellants contended that once the certificate was granted, the Supreme Court was automatically obligated to hear their appeal as an ordinary appellate court, on both facts and law.
law: Article 134(1)(c) grants the High Court the discretion to certify that a case is a fit one for appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court has general powers of judicial superintendence over all courts in India and is the ultimate interpreter of the Constitution.
The discretion granted to the High Court under Article 134(1)(c) is a judicial one and must be exercised along well-established legal principles.
application: The Supreme Court asserted that the mere grant of a certificate does not prevent it from determining whether the certificate was rightly granted and if the necessary conditions were met.
The Court found that the High Court had misdirected itself about the law. It wrongly believed its discretion was fettered and that it had no option but to grant the certificate to all the convicts.
The Court clarified that the word 'case' in Article 134(1)(c) refers to the case of each individual person, not the appeal as a whole.
Because the High Court did not properly exercise its judicial discretion, the Supreme Court held that it was not bound by the wrongly issued certificate.

The Court distinguished a Federal Court precedent cited by the appellants, stating it dealt with a different law (the Government of India Act, 1935) that used different language and was therefore not applicable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the grant of a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) does not automatically obligate it to hear an appeal. The Court retains the power to determine if the certificate was properly granted and can interfere if the High Court failed to exercise its judicial discretion correctly.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the grant of a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) automatically obligates the Supreme Court to hear the appeal on both facts and law, as an ordinary court of appeal.
appellant_arguments: Having obtained a certificate, the Supreme Court becomes an ordinary Court of appeal and is bound to hear the case on both facts and law.

respondent_arguments: The respondent's implicit argument is that the certificate does not bind the Supreme Court to hear the appeal on its merits. The court retains its usual discretion to dismiss the appeal if it finds no substance in it, just as it would with a petition for special leave.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The mere grant of a certificate by a High Court under Article 134(1)(c) does not preclude the Supreme Court from determining whether the certificate was rightly granted. The discretion of the High Court to grant such a certificate is a judicial one, and if the High Court misdirects itself on the law and fails to exercise that discretion, the Supreme Court can review and invalidate the certificate.
obiter: The Supreme Court has general powers of judicial superintendence over all Courts in India and is the ultimate interpreter and guardian of the Constitution.
If a High Court's judicial discretion is properly exercised on well-established and proper lines, the Supreme Court will not interfere except on very strong grounds.
A certificate must show on its face that the discretion conferred was invoked and exercised.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The mere grant of a certificate of fitness for appeal by a High Court under Article 134(1)(c) does not preclude the Supreme Court from determining whether it was rightly granted. The discretion to grant such a certificate is a judicial one that must be exercised along well-established lines. If the High Court misdirects itself on the law and fails to properly exercise this discretion, the Supreme Court can interfere and dismiss the appeal if the certificate was wrongly granted.
legal_tests_applied: The discretion to grant a certificate under Article 134(1)(c) is a judicial one and must be judicially exercised along the well established lines which govern these matters.

If, on the face of the order, it is apparent that the Court has misdirected itself and considered that its discretion was fettered when it was not, or that it had none, then the superior Court must either remit the case or exercise the discretion itself.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's contention that obtaining a certificate transforms the Supreme Court into an ordinary Court of appeal bound to hear the case on facts and law was rejected. The Federal Court precedent cited was distinguished as it dealt with a different law (section 205 of the Government of India Act, 1935) that did not use the same or similar words.

The High Court granted the certificate not because the appellants' cases had merit, but because it misdirected itself about the law, believing it had no discretion or that its discretion was fettered regarding the meaning of the word 'case'.

The certificate was wrongly granted because, as the High Court itself noted, there was 'nothing of an exceptional nature in their cases.' Had the appellants sought special leave, their petition would have been dismissed.
why_respondent_won: The Supreme Court has the authority to review the validity of a certificate, as the mere grant 'would not preclude this Court from determining whether it was rightly granted and whether the conditions prerequisite to the grant are satisfied.'

The High Court's discretion under Article 134(1)(c) is a judicial one that must be properly exercised. In this instance, the High Court 'misdirected themselves about the law and as a consequence did not exercise the discretion which is vested in them.'

Because the High Court failed to properly exercise its judicial discretion, the Supreme Court was bound to interfere, leading to the conclusion that the certificate was wrongly granted and the appeal must fail.
policy_considerations: This Court has general powers of judicial superintendence over all Courts in India and is the ultimate interpreter and guardian of the Constitution.
It has a duty to see that its provisions are faithfully observed and, where necessary, to expound them.
